chains.title: Ref T preserves a HOXB13 site in the 6q22 enhancer, raising RFX6 expression in prostate cells

links.claim: QBiC-SELEX gives HOXB13 its own model with the largest effect in the screen (z -103.49, effect -4.771; ref 99.9th vs alt 97.2th percentile k-mer strength), so ref T is predicted to bind more. Within Homeodomain group G024 (HOXA13/C13/D13 share the specificity) HOXB13 is chosen because it is by far the most expressed member in LNCaP (182.31 vs 4.13, 0.01, 0.01 TPM) and is the prostate master TF reported in a complex at this enhancer. This is an in vitro prediction only: no allele-specific HOXB13 assay is shown, and Factorbook finds no HOXB13 peak containing the variant in LNCaP-matching biosamples (absence may reflect no experiment).

The variant lies in a distal enhancer-like cCRE with DNase/H3K27ac signal (z-scores are maxima over biosamples, not LNCaP-specific), described in the literature as the rs339331/6q22 prostate risk enhancer carrying a HOXB13-containing complex.

The enhancer is assigned to RFX6: the variant is intronic to RFX6, RFX6 has the nearest TSS, L2G scores RFX6 highest (0.87, though 0.27-0.87 across sets), and GATA2/SMAD4/HOXB13 at this enhancer are reported to increase RFX6 expression. No GTEx prostate eQTL is significant for this variant, so the steady-state effect in normal prostate is small or absent.
HOXB13 is highly expressed in LNCaP (182.31 TPM) and the enhancer is described as an AR/HOXB13-associated site in prostate tumors; LNCaP-specific chromatin tracks are not shown here.

The locus is a genome-wide significant prostate cancer risk locus (p 5e-20) and RFX6 dysregulation is reported to affect tumour proliferation, migration and prognosis; the allele-to-RFX6-to-phenotype step is not directly demonstrated in the cited quotes.

chains.title: Ref T strengthens a reprogrammed androgen receptor binding site, increasing AR-driven RFX6 output
chains.element: cCRE EH38E2496909 / reprogrammed AR binding site at rs339331

links.claim: Published functional work reports rs339331 lies in a reprogrammed AR binding site with the T risk allele enhancing AR chromatin occupancy. QBiC-SELEX lookup shows AR has its own model, but it does not pass the gate at this site (z 0.94, p 0.35) and its small effect is positive (alt slightly favoured); only the CIS-BP-mapped NR3C2 model passes (effect +0.811, alt binds more). So in vitro motif data do not support, and mildly oppose, a T-favoured direct AR contact: the reported T-allele AR gain is more likely indirect, via a cooperating pioneer factor (e.g. HOXB13/GATA2) rather than direct AR half-site change.
The same distal enhancer-like cCRE harbours the reported AR site and carries active enhancer marks.
Enhancer activity at this site is reported to drive RFX6 (shown for the GATA2/SMAD4/HOXB13 complex, not for AR directly); RFX6 is also the host gene and top L2G gene.
AR reprogramming to this site is reported in prostate tumours; LNCaP is AR-positive but is not named in the quoted evidence and AR occupancy there is untested.
The inherited allele is reported to confer prostate cancer progression and drug resistance via RFX6/HOXA10-orchestrated TGFbeta signalling, at a locus associated with prostate cancer at p 5e-20.

chains.title: Ref T preserves a posterior-HOX (HOXA10/HOXC6-type) site; alt C weakens it, altering RFX6 output

links.claim: Homeodomain group G004 (18 concordant passing models, best HOXC10 z -84.28, effect -4.457; ref 100th vs alt 89.4th percentile) predicts the alt C allele binds this posterior-HOX specificity less. This is a group-level specificity, not one TF: I name HOXA10 because it has its own model and is expressed in LNCaP (4.23 TPM) and is the RFX6 partner named downstream in the literature, but HOXC6 (18.43 TPM, mapped), MNX1 (8.35) and HOXC12 (6.33) are better-expressed alternatives that the motif cannot distinguish. No allele-specific occupancy data exist for any of them.
The affected k-mer lies inside the active distal enhancer-like cCRE containing the variant; no direct evidence places a posterior-HOX site there.
The enhancer is assigned to RFX6 by host-gene status, proximity and L2G, with no HOXA10-specific link to RFX6 from this element.
Posterior HOX factors are expressed in LNCaP (HOXC6 18.43, MNX1 8.35, HOXA10 4.23 TPM), but expression does not demonstrate occupancy.
The locus associates with prostate cancer (p 5e-20) and an RFX6/HOXA10 TGFbeta axis is reported downstream; no quote links posterior-HOX binding at this allele to phenotype.

Allelic enhancer activity persists after HOXB13 depletion but is lost after posterior-HOX knockdown
falsified_if: No posterior-HOX factor occupies the enhancer in prostate cells
Knockdown of HOXA10/HOXC6 leaves RFX6 and enhancer activity unchanged

chains.title: Alt C creates an IRF-family (IRF3/IRF6) binding site that alters enhancer activity

links.claim: Several IRF models score positively at this site (IRF3 own model, z 44.89, effect 2.092, ref 80.5th to alt 100th percentile; IRF6 own model z 56.39). IRF3 is chosen because it is the most expressed IRF in LNCaP (54.41 TPM) and has its own model; IRF6 (38.37 TPM) cannot be excluded from motif data alone. The predicted direction (alt binds more) is opposite to the published T-risk-allele AR/HOXB13 mechanism.
A gained IRF site would fall in the active distal enhancer-like cCRE containing the variant; no IRF footprint is documented there.
Changed enhancer activity would act on RFX6, the host and top L2G gene; no IRF-RFX6 link is shown, and no prostate eQTL is detected.
IRF3 is abundantly expressed in LNCaP (54.41 TPM), consistent with but not demonstrating occupancy.
C is the GWAS risk allele for prostate cancer (p 5e-20) and RFX6 dysregulation is linked to tumour behaviour generally.

grades_v0.reason: QBiC-SELEX (E07/E08) shows ref binds HOXB13 more (z -103.49), a prediction only. E06d says HOXB13 is in a complex at the enhancer but does not give an allelic HOXB13 effect. E06c says AR occupancy is enhanced by T, not HOXB13. No ChIP or reporter shows HOXB13 allelic binding.
E03 places the variant in the dELS cCRE, though the z-scores are maxima over biosamples. E06c/E06d describe it as the rs339331/6q22 enhancer, an AR site with a HOXB13 complex.

E06d reports increased RFX6 expression via this enhancer, and E05 gives L2G 0.87 for RFX6. Proximity (E01/E02) is only weak support. No eQTL or CRISPR evidence is cited, and the L2G is lower in other credible sets.

HOXB13 expression of 182 TPM in LNCaP (E08) and AR/HOXB13 co-occupancy in prostate tumors are consistent with the claim. Prostate specificity is not tested, and the cCRE z-scores are not biosample-specific.

E04 gives a GWAS association at p 5e-20, and E06a/E06b are consistent with an RFX6 role in cancer. No quote shows that RFX6 levels change proliferation or TGFb signalling via this allele, and the review is general.

E06c is a functional literature quote that the T risk allele enhances AR chromatin occupancy, which fits the T-binds-more direction. It is not an independent allelic assay shown here, and AR coverage is not checked.
E03 gives the cCRE with enhancer marks, and E06c places the AR site at rs339331.
E06d links the enhancer to RFX6 expression via GATA2/SMAD4/HOXB13, not AR. L2G (E05) and proximity support RFX6, but the AR-driven effect on RFX6 is not shown.
E06c reports the AR site in prostate tumors. LNCaP is not named in the evidence, and AR expression in the context is not checked.
E06b (title in E06) supports the RFX6/HOXA10 TGFb progression route, but the AR-to-RFX6-to-phenotype step is not shown, and the cited quote only gives the locus association.

G004 is a group-level prediction only. HOXA10 is picked from 18 models without a reason beyond 4.23 TPM. E06b does not name HOXA10 as binding the site, only RFX6/HOXA10 TGFb signalling, and a downstream partner is not binding evidence. HOXA10 has no allele-specific data.
E03 shows the variant is in the cCRE, but there is no evidence that a posterior HOX site lies there.
E02/E05 give proximity and L2G for RFX6, but no HOXA10-specific link to RFX6 expression from this enhancer.
E09 shows HOXA10 at 4.23 TPM, which is low, and expression alone does not show occupancy.
E06b/E04 support the locus and the RFX6/HOXA10 TGFb axis only by title. There is no quote linking HOXA10 binding at this allele to phenotype.

The IRF3 gain (z 44.89) is a QBiC prediction alone. IRF3 is chosen over IRF6 by TPM, and IRF3 is a poor fit to a prostate enhancer. The direction (alt binds more) is opposite to the published T-risk-allele AR/HOXB13 mechanism.
E03 supports the cCRE location, but there is no evidence of an IRF site there.
RFX6 is assigned by L2G and host gene only. There is no evidence that IRF3 acts on RFX6.
E12 shows 54 TPM IRF3 expression, which is consistent but gives no occupancy evidence.
E04 shows C is the GWAS risk allele, which is consistent with the direction, but E06a is a generic RFX6 statement and there is no IRF-specific link.

grades_final.reason: E08 gives a HOXB13 own-model prediction (z -103.49, ref binds more), which is only a binding prediction. E06d places HOXB13 in a complex at the enhancer but gives no allele-specific data. E19 finds no HOXB13 peak in LNCaP. The TF choice within G024 is justified by expression and literature. Direction is consistent with the T-risk-allele literature.

E03 shows the variant inside dELS cCRE EH38E2496909 with DNase and H3K27ac signal (maxima over biosamples, not LNCaP-specific). E06d names rs339331/6q22 as a risk enhancer with a HOXB13-containing complex.

E06d reports the GATA2/SMAD4/HOXB13 complex at this enhancer increasing RFX6 expression, and E05 gives L2G 0.87 for RFX6 with E01/E02 showing proximity. No quoted perturbation (CRISPR or reporter) shows this exact variant or enhancer changes RFX6. E20 shows no prostate eQTL. Spread of L2G across sets (0.27-0.87) is noted. Direction of the effect on RFX6 for the allele is not shown.

HOXB13 is highly expressed (182 TPM in LNCaP, E08) and E06c/E06d tie the site to prostate tumours, but LNCaP is not named in the quotes. E19 shows no HOXB13 peak in LNCaP. No LNCaP chromatin tracks are cited.

E04 gives a GWAS association at p 5e-20 and E06b ties the locus to prostate cancer risk. E06a reports general RFX6 dysregulation effects. The allele-to-RFX6-to-phenotype chain is not directly shown in the quotes, as the chain itself admits.

E06c is a literature quote that the T allele enhances AR chromatin occupancy, which is an experimental observation consistent with ref binding more. However, E18 shows AR's own model fails the gate (z 0.94) with a slight positive alt effect, and only mapped NR3C2 passes in the opposite direction. The chain's indirect-mechanism explanation is speculative. Coverage own_model for AR is verified by E18.
E03 shows the variant in an active dELS cCRE, and E06c places it in a reprogrammed AR binding site in tumours.
The RFX6 link rests on E06d, which concerns the GATA2/SMAD4/HOXB13 complex, not AR, plus host-gene status and L2G in E01/E05. No AR-specific link to RFX6 is shown, as the claim itself acknowledges.
E06c reports AR reprogramming in prostate tumours, but LNCaP is not named, and no AR ChIP in LNCaP is cited. LNCaP's AR positivity comes from background knowledge, not the provided evidence.

E04 gives the GWAS association, and E06b supports the locus-prostate cancer link. The progression/drug-resistance via RFX6/HOXA10-TGFb claim comes from the PMID 38932472 title in E06, not a quote of mechanism, so it is only consistent.

E09 shows a group-level prediction for posterior HOX (z -84.28, alt binds less) and E07 indicates the screen. HOXA10 is chosen partly because of an RFX6 partnership claim rather than binding evidence, and better-expressed alternatives exist. There is no occupancy data. The chosen TF is weakly justified, but this is disclosed.
E03 supports the cCRE containing the variant, but nothing places a posterior-HOX site or occupancy there, as the claim concedes.
Host gene, proximity and L2G (E01/E02/E05) support RFX6 as the likely target, but this is not specific to HOXA10 and there is no perturbation evidence.
E09 gives expression TPMs of the HOX factors in LNCaP, which is context only and does not show occupancy.
E04 shows the GWAS association and E06b supports the locus. The RFX6/HOXA10 axis comes from a literature title, but no quote links posterior-HOX binding at this allele to phenotype.

E12 and E10 give positive IRF3/IRF6 predictions (alt binds more), but this is binding prediction alone. IRF3 is chosen via expression with IRF6 acknowledged as a possible alternative. No IRF experimental data are cited. The direction is opposite to the published T-allele mechanism.
E03 supports the cCRE, but no IRF footprint is shown, as acknowledged.
The RFX6 assignment relies on host gene and L2G (E01/E05) only. No IRF-RFX6 link exists, and E20 shows no prostate eQTL.
E12 shows IRF3 expression in LNCaP (54.41 TPM), consistent with but not demonstrating occupancy.

E04 shows the C risk allele GWAS association, and E06a gives generic RFX6 tumour effects. The IRF-mediated link to phenotype is not shown, and the direction conflicts with the published T-risk mechanism in E06c, so the chain is weakly consistent at best.

Dysregulated expression or mutations of the RFX6 gene in prostate cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, gastric cancer, melanoma, and other tumors have garnered significant interest, with studies showing that such alterations affect tumor cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, and are correlated with an unfavorable clinical prognosis in patients carrying RFX6 mutations.

Here the FinnGen cohort phenome-wide analysis, along with multiple genome-wide association studies, has consistently identified the rs339331-RFX6/6q22 locus associated with prostate cancer (PCa) risk across diverse populations.
It is uncovered that rs339331 resides in a reprogrammed androgen receptor (AR) binding site in PCa tumors, with the T risk allele enhancing AR chromatin occupancy.

Strinkingly, GATA2 and SMAD4 globally mediated inherited PCa risk and formed a transcriptional complex with HOXB13 at the PCa risk-associated rs339331/6q22 enhancer, leading to increased expression of the PCa susceptibility gene RFX6.
Notable genes of interest include HCP5, RFX6 and H3C1 for risk, and MKI67 and KLF5 for aggressive disease.
